ch5_ex5_q1a: Avoid dividing altogether: the other acute angle is $90^\circ - 71^\circ = 19^\circ$, and from there $m$ is opposite, so $m = 2.3\tan(19^\circ) \approx 0.79$, the same answer.
Estimate check: $71^\circ$ is a big angle, so the side opposite it (2.3 m) must be much longer than $m$. An answer under 1 m makes sense.
ch5_ex5_q1b: For small angles $\cos\theta$ is close to 1 ($\cos 13^\circ \approx 0.97$), so the hypotenuse is only a little longer than the adjacent side. Expect an answer just above 4.6.
Memory aid: SOH CAH TOA, or "Some Old Horses Can Always Hear Their Owners Approach".
ch5_ex5_q1c: Since $\sin 68^\circ \approx 0.93$, the hypotenuse is about $94 \div 0.93$, a bit more than 100 mm. That quick estimate confirms 101.38.
Cover-up triangle: put O on top and S, H underneath. Cover H and you see $H = \dfrac{O}{S}$.
ch5_ex5_q2a: $60^\circ$ is a special angle: $\sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, so $a = 10 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 5\sqrt{3}$ exactly, which is about 8.660.
Half an equilateral triangle with side 10 has sides 5, $5\sqrt{3}$ and 10. That is a picture of this exact triangle.
ch5_ex5_q2b: Estimate: $\cos 25^\circ$ is about 0.9, so $a \approx 0.9 \times 8 = 7.2$. The exact 7.250 is close, so the setup is right.
The adjacent side is the leg that touches the angle and is not the hypotenuse, so here it is the base.
ch5_ex5_q2c: Tan connects the two legs, so whenever the hypotenuse is neither given nor asked for, reach for tan.
ch5_ex5_q3a: Convert minutes by hand: $26' = \dfrac{26}{60} \approx 0.433^\circ$, so the angle is about $40.433^\circ$. Think of it like time: 26 minutes is not 0.26 of an hour.
ch5_ex5_q3b: For small angles, $\tan\theta$ is close to the angle in radians. $8^\circ 52' 45'' \approx 0.155$ rad, so $P \approx 11.7 \div 0.155 \approx 75$, a good check.
A small angle means the side opposite it is short, so the adjacent side $P$ should be several times longer than 11.7.
ch5_ex5_q3c: Since $\sin 18^\circ \approx 0.31$, the hypotenuse is roughly $14 \div 0.31 \approx 45$ m, which matches 44.82.
A small angle with a given opposite side always gives a long hypotenuse, here about three times the opposite side.
ch5_ex5_q4a: The angle is below $45^\circ$, so the opposite side $x$ must be shorter than the adjacent side, 11.2 mm.
ch5_ex5_q4b: On many calculators the DMS key is marked $^\circ\,'\,''$. Type $21$ [DMS] $25$ [DMS] $34$ [DMS] and then press cos.
ch5_ex5_q4c: Small-angle check: $\sin\theta \approx \theta$ in radians. $6^\circ 25' \approx 0.112$ rad, so $x \approx 80.9 \times 0.112 \approx 9.06$, very close to 9.04.
ch5_ex5_q5a: Find the side opposite an angle by looking straight across the triangle from that angle. From the bottom vertex you look across to the top side, $x$.
ch5_ex5_q5b: The angle is under $45^\circ$, so $y$ (opposite) must be shorter than 23.7 (adjacent).
ch5_ex5_q5c: Check with tan: the third side is $12.3\tan(34^\circ 12') \approx 8.36$, and $\sqrt{12.3^2 + 8.36^2} \approx 14.87$ agrees with $z$.
ch5_ex5_q6a: Since $\sin 13^\circ \approx 0.23$, $p \approx 15.3 \div 0.23 \approx 67$. A small angle makes the hypotenuse several times the opposite side.
ch5_ex5_q6b: Pythagoras check: $21.38^2 + 42.29^2 \approx 2245.5$ and $47.385^2 \approx 2245.3$. These agree up to rounding.
The angle is over $45^\circ$, so the side opposite it ($q$) should be longer than the adjacent side ($p$). It is.
ch5_ex5_q6c: Shortcut: once you have $a$, you could get $b$ from Pythagoras, $b = \sqrt{0.732^2 - a^2}$. Using cos directly avoids rounding errors, though.
$\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ are just the fractions of the hypotenuse taken up by each leg. Here $a$ is about 96% of it and $b$ about 29%.
ch5_ex5_q7a: Because $42^\circ < 45^\circ$, $\sin 42^\circ < \cos 42^\circ$, so the opposite side must come out shorter than the adjacent side in part b.
ch5_ex5_q7b: Link: $\cos 42^\circ = \sin 48^\circ$, because the other acute angle is $48^\circ$. The side adjacent to one angle is opposite the other.
Pythagoras check: $6.0^2 + 6.7^2 \approx 80.9$ and $8.95^2 \approx 80.1$. That is close, and the gap comes from rounding.
ch5_ex5_q8: Estimate: $\tan 35^\circ \approx 0.7$, so the height is about $0.7 \times 1.5 = 1.05$ m.
Sketch the wall, ground and ladder as a right triangle first. The ground distance touches the angle, so it is the adjacent side.
ch5_ex5_q9a: Check that $x > y$: the sloping top is the hypotenuse of the side view, so it must be longer than the base.
ch5_ex5_q9b: The top, bottom and back rectangles all share the width $z$, so factor it out: area $= z(x + y + 8) + 2 \times \tfrac{1}{2} \times 8y$. Fewer multiplications means fewer slips.
Picture unfolding the box into a net to make sure every face is counted once: 3 rectangles and 2 triangles.
ch5_ex5_q10a: Since $\tan\theta = \dfrac{O}{A}$, equal sides mean $\tan\theta = 1$, and $\tan 45^\circ = 1$. Try it on your calculator.
Link: this is the $45^\circ$-$45^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle with sides $1, 1, \sqrt{2}$, half of a square cut along its diagonal.
ch5_ex5_q10b: Adjacent longer than opposite means $\tan\theta < 1$. Tan increases from 0 at $0^\circ$ to 1 at $45^\circ$, so the answer is $\theta < 45^\circ$.
ch5_ex5_q11: Spot the error with logic: $\tan 29^\circ < 1$, so the adjacent side $MC$ must be longer than $AM = 2.645$. Jack's $MC \approx 1.47$ is too short.
Since $\angle C$ is smaller than $\angle B$, $C$ is further from the foot $M$, so $MC$ should be longer than $BM$.
ch5_ex5_q12a: Two-angle problems always give two expressions for the same height. Write both, then set them equal; that is the plan for part b.
ch5_ex5_q12b: General pattern: $x = \dfrac{64\tan(36^\circ 24')}{\tan(47^\circ 48') - \tan(36^\circ 24')}$. Type this as one calculator expression with brackets to keep full accuracy.
Check: substitute $x \approx 129.07$ into both expressions. Each gives $h \approx 142.34$ m.
ch5_ex5_q12c: Units trap: the eye level is 195 cm, which is $1.95$ m. Adding 195 instead would give an absurd building height.
ch5_ex5_q13: The angle of depression from B equals the angle of elevation from A's top (alternate angles), so both triangles share the 110 m horizontal leg.
Estimate: $\tan 15^\circ \approx 0.27$ and $\tan 22^\circ \approx 0.4$, giving about 30 m and $30 + 44 \approx 74$ m.
ch5_ex5_q14: A $45^\circ$ right triangle has equal legs, so $NP = h$ immediately. With $\tan 30^\circ = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, $MN = h\sqrt{3}$, and $3h^2 + h^2 = 120^2$ gives $h = 60$.
Exact values for $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ often make 3D problems come out as whole numbers. Use them instead of decimals.
ch5_ex5_q15: Rule of thumb: finding a leg means multiply by the ratio, and finding the hypotenuse means divide by sin or cos. Because sin and cos are below 1, dividing makes the answer larger, as a hypotenuse should be.
